THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 


YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


This year's intense activity was driven by the major objectives of our 
2005-2008 Strategic Plan: consolidating our organization, increasing 
the reach of our programs and promoting a better understanding of 
Our mission. 


We acquired a new computer system, thereby ensuring better member- 
ship follow-up. We managed our finances carefully and responsibly, 
which will help us implement an extensive re-investment plan in our 
Pointe-St-Charles and Kanawana facilities. 


With respect to our programs, we actively participated in a study on the 
needs of an aging population. Our Innovation Fund enabled us to launch 
a wide range of new community programs, such as support for new 
mothers and assistance for homeless Aboriginals. We also developed 
tools to evaluate the quality and relevance of our community programs. 


Lastly, we stepped up efforts to promote the role of the YMCA of Greater 
Montreal in society. At the local level, we renewed ties with our neigh- 
bours and friends, especially those at Camp YMCA Kanawana. On the 
international level, we helped organize a conference on solidarity in 
action. 


Each of these decisions and actions were motivated by our ongoing deter- 
mination to reach more people and to advance the five fundamental 
values of the YMCA: volunteer work and philanthropy, participation and 
access, self-empowerment, education and prevention, and respect for 
others. These five values are what make the YMCA of Greater Montreal a 
unique, open and friendly place. The profiles presented here portray five 
members of our large family who exemplify our values. 


These values are also evidenced in the daily cooperation between our 
volunteers and staff who work together to achieve our objectives. The 
remarkable contribution of our hundreds of volunteers is visible every- 
where — in the weight training room, on the board of directors and local 
committees, as well as in community and international programs. 


We wish to thank all our volunteers, donors and staff. Your involvement 
and cooperation make all the difference. 


Christian Charbonneau Stéphane Vaillancourt 
Chair of the Board of Directors President and Chief 
Executive Officer

THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION INC. 


Of the YMCA’s five core values, volunteer work and philanthropy conti- 
nue to be the cornerstone of its social mission. In this respect, the YMCA 
of Greater Montreal Foundation works alongside the YMCA to support 
key initiatives that will enable us to reach out to and better serve our 
communities. 


Whether to improve our facilities or build new ones, support the deve- 
lopment of a new project or ensure the continuity of a successful pro- 
gram, the Foundation’s many volunteers and donors enable us to go from 
dream to reality. 


As part of our annual campaigns, dozens of volunteers in each of our 
centres joined forces to raise more than $230,000 this year. These dona- 
tions will enable us to welcome special needs children in our day camps, 
deliver hot meals to an underprivileged school, help refugees integrate 
into Canadian society and meet a whole range of other current needs. 


With an eye to the future, Foundation Board Members generously 
invested their time and money in the YMCA Endowment Fund, which 
grew by more than $600,000 to $4,367,078 as at May 31, 2005. This resul- 
ted in a significant increase in endowment income, which is used to sup- 
port numerous community programs every year. Indeed, the Endowment 
Fund provides stable and predictable revenues, thereby enabling com- 
munity programs to carry on and grow in spite of the uncertainty asso- 
ciated with other sources of funding. 


We remain convinced that developing the Endowment Fund is an essen- 
tial step in ensuring the sustainability of the YMCA’s community action. 
We wish to thank all those who showed their trust in the YMCA by 
investing in the Endowment Fund, either through an outright gift or a 
future pledge. This trust is one of our greatest assets and will be care- 
fully nurtured and preserved through solid and responsible management 
of the Fund. 


The YMCA has always promoted volunteer work and philanthropy as 
essential components of personal development, leadership and a sense 
of belonging to the community. These are key aspects of overall perso- 
nal growth—an approach symbolized by the famous “spirit, mind and 
body” triangle, which is part of the logo of all YMCAs around the world. 


Our sincere thanks to all who so generously share their spirit with us.

Although Johanne Gordian is optimistic about life today, it has not 
always been the case. After a divorce, she found herself alone with her 
two sons, one of whom had problems. He lacked self-confidence, was 
depressed and aggressive. At the early age of 12, he started taking 
drugs. At age 13, just before the year-end exams, he was suspended 
from school for six weeks with no other options. 


Johanne knocked on a lot of doors until someone told her about the 
Alternative Suspension program at the West Island YMCA. Her son met 
different and “smart” adults there, she said, with whom he built relation- 
ships of trust. In addition to taking courses, he had a chance to talk 
about his problems one-on-one and in groups. When the six weeks were 
up, he continued going to the YMCA practically every day. He felt com- 
fortable, appreciated and well supported—so much so that after a major 
fight with his mother, he took refuge there. That day, the youth workers 
sat down with the mother and son and encouraged them to not only talk, 
but to sign a contract of mutual respect, which was a turning point in 
their relationship. “The YMCA provided tremendous help to my child and 
helped me as well,” she said. 


Three years and a few wrong turns later, the youth took charge of his life. 
He was determined to succeed, studied hard, stopped taking drugs and 
broke all ties with people who could have a negative influence on him. 
His ambition is to one day become a youth worker. Johanne Gordian can 
finally relax now. She speaks about her 16-year-old teen with great pride. 


“If that child becomes an honest citizen, it's because the Y helped me. | 
take my hat off to the two youth workers who took care of us. Sometimes 
it doesn't take much to influence a youth one way or another. But it takes 
time... three years in our case.”

PEOPLE WITH STRONG VALUES 


“/ Tf the model of the world was built on the Kanawana 
model, and if we could all live in such a peaceful place in the mid- 
dle of nature, life would definitely be a lot better for everyone. /’ 


AYUNDA DUBE 


A native of Zimbabwe, Ayunda Dube arrived in Montreal as a refugee at 
the age of 19. He found his first home away from home and contacts at 
the Downtown YMCA—something he hasn't forgotten. Three years later, 
he was asked to become a counsellor at Camp YMCA Kanawana. He 
agreed without hesitation, and was only too happy to do something in 
return for what the YMCA had done for him. 


“After having said ‘yes’, | was scared—scared of being the only black 
guy at the camp— and of not being accepted by the other counsellors.” 
Since he had never been to a summer camp, he was afraid that he 
wouldn't know what to do with the children. 


On the first day of camp, his initial fears were immediately dispelled. The 
counsellors came from all over in the world. There were no racial or cul- 
tural distinctions in the group. “At Kanawana, the only culture that exists 
is the camp culture. We are all Kanawanians.” This totally new experi- 
ence for him gave rise to sincere and lasting friendships. 


As for the children... “As soon as | saw them, something immediately 
kicked in. During our counsellor training workshop, they said to try and 
give something special to the kids, something nobody else could give 
them. | thought to myself; I'm just going to be myself. | am from Africa, so 
what | am going to give those children is Africa.” It worked like a charm. 
They were curious and wanted to know everything about him and his life 
in Africa. 


Ayunda Dube dreams of going back to Camp YMCA Kanawana for its 
atmosphere of respect, and because it's such a beautiful place. He felt 
accepted and more at home than anywhere else. “If the model of the 
world was built on the Kanawana model, and if we could all live in such 
a peaceful place in the middle of nature, life would definitely be a lot bet- 
ter for everyone.” 


YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


2004-2005

something that is learned. Through 
workshops and meetings, the /mpact

become aware of the effect of their 


actions.

Fred Francis started going to the YMCA to get into shape. After two days 
of training alone, he joined a fitness class. He was soon captivated by 
the friendly and dynamic atmosphere at the YMCA. 


Twenty years later, he’s still there as a volunteer. “When | was asked if | 
wanted to become an instructor, | said ‘yes’. | felt it was really important 
at that point in time to start giving back what | had received from the 
YMCA.” Since then, Fred has always gladly agreed when asked to join a 
committee or work on a fund-raising campaign. Sometimes he sponta- 
neously helps out at the front desk when he sees that staff are really 
busy. 


As a tireless ambassador for the YMCA, he gets his motivation from “life 
outside the gym”, as he says it so well. For him, life outside the gym is 
the people he meets on a daily basis and the YMCA‘s numerous commu- 
nity programs that improve so many lives. He is fond of saying, “the Y is 
so much more than a gym.” Over the years, Fred discovered aspects of 
the YMCA that are not well known by most people who use its facilities. 
First and foremost, there's the YMCA family where he has built solid 
friendships. Secondly, there's the whole range of YMCA community 
services. 


This is what he talks about when he’s fund-raising. “My objective is not 
so much to ask for money, but to explain the broad scope of the YMCA‘s 
action and its role in society. When people find out how important the 
centres are to the local community, they make a donation.” Fred takes 
every opportunity to talk about the YMCA, whether to people that he 
meets in the hallway, locker room (his “second office”) or even the sauna. 


“The YMCA has given so much to me. My health, of course... But, above 
all, it has given me the opportunity to meet wonderful people and dis- 
cover a true community environment. By volunteering at the Y, | feel like 
I'm giving back to the Y what | have received a hundred times over.” 


YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


2004-2005 


In all the centres combined, 1,450 vol- 
unteers donate their time and energy, 
thereby contributing to the YMCA‘s 
community action. 


The YMCA would not be able to play 
such an important role in society 
without the generosity of more than 
900 donors who contribute to annual 
fund-raising campaigns and to the 
permanent YMCA Endowment Fund. 


YMCA volunteer work extends well 
beyond the centres’ walls. For exam- 
ple, volunteers at the Guy-Favreau 
YMCA have formed a strong partner- 
ship with a school in an underprivi- 
leged neighbourhood. Among other 
things, volunteers ensure that stu- 
dents have all the school supplies and 
clothes they need.

JONATHAN AYOTTE 


PARTICIPATION 
AND ACCESS 


At the age of 12, Jonathan Ayotte is already a ‘regular’ at the Pointe-St- 
Charles YMCA. He joined the Y when he was 8 years old, where he dis- 
covered various sports, including soccer and basketball. He recently 
took a more intensive basketball course subsidized by the Canadian Tire 
JumpStart program. The aim of the program is to use physical activity to 
give all youth an equal chance at acquiring the social skills and self- 
esteem they will need throughout their lives. As such, the program puts 
YMCA values in action and demonstrates our ability to build partner- 
ships for the benefit of the community. 


Jonathan also goes to the YMCA Homework Club—a program that aims 
to give all youth an opportunity to grow and develop their full potential. 
“If you need help, you can always find a tutor. They helped me a lot with 
my math and other subjects too. | think that I'll go on to the homework 
program for teenagers.” 


Jonathan intends to continue his activities at the YMCA. He loves the 
Youth Zone, which offers a wide range of activities and is a great meet- 
ing place. “At school, they tell you what to do. At the YMCA, they have 
tons of activities, and you can choose the ones you want.” He is impa- 
tiently awaiting the next round of basketball courses. In fact, his dream 
is to become a pro, just like the former Globetrotters player who came 
to speak about his career and passion for basketball with teenagers at 
the YMCA. 


Inthe meantime, Jonathan is already showing leadership skills by occa- 
sionally volunteering to help the Youth Zone monitors. 


“It's a great place to go after school. You just learn so much!”

Christine Ligondé is a very active retired teacher, who is also very inde- 
pendent. For her, health is the key to independence and self-empower- 
ment. She works out most days and encourages others to join her in a 
whole range of activities. For close to five years, she has actively 
volunteered at the Saint-Laurent YMCA on the local board of directors, 
for annual fund-raising campaigns and as a facilitator. She enjoys 
helping the people around her feel happy. 


In cooperation with staff members, she launched “Between Friends”. 
The purpose of the group is to reach isolated individuals and encourage 
them to get out of the house, get moving, learn new things and actively 
participate in community life. “There are a lot of grandparents who 
immigrated here with their children and grandchildren. They are often 
isolated and face real language barriers. You have to start by finding 
them, then bring them out of their shell and teach them French or 
English.” 


For Christine, learning opportunities abound, as evidenced by the wide 
variety of activities available to her group: computer courses, French 
and English courses, physical activity, intercultural community meals, 
Christmas carols and suppers, arts and crafts, recycling of old jewellery, 
painting, meetings with counsellors... Afraid of going out in the 
evening? Not to worry! She invites a police officer to provide tips and 
tricks for safe travel. For those who really can’t or don’t dare go out 
alone, the centre has an old minibus to pick them up. 


She thinks the YMCA is the best place for this type of group. Granted, it 
may be part of its mission, she says, but also because people of all 
nationalities are already there. “I call the YMCA my United Nations.” It's 
a perfect place to gain self-confidence and broaden your horizons. 


YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


2004-2005 


To enable seniors who live alone to 
stay at home as long as possible and 
give them a sense of security, the 
PAIR Program calls them every day to 
be sure they are all right. 


Through its International Programs, 
the YMCA of Greater Montreal gives 
communities abroad the resources 
and help they need to take charge of 
and improve their destiny. 


To navigate our legal system, you 
need to know the law. Several centres 
have set up a legal clinic for people 
with problems related to criminal, 
family, immigration law, etc.

SOCIAL AUDIT OF THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


In 2004-2005, the YMCA of Greater Montreal facilitated access to its programs 
and facilities for more than 5,424 people who were in financial difficulty. 


Through its programs and activities, the YMCA of Greater Montreal also 
reached 159,821 people in 2004-2005. 


This social audit is made possible through the exceptional dedication of 
our 1,450 volunteers and staff of 1,250.

INNOVATION, RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT FUND 


2004-2005 


In 2003, the YMCA of Greater Montreal created a fund to increase the reach of its programs and services. With 
new resources of $150,000 again this year, the Fund has supported the implementation of new initiatives, as 
well as projects that aim to maintain the relevance, efficiency and quality of the YMCA’s actions. The projects 
selected meet strict criteria based on the YMCA’s mission and their level of integration into the community. 
Projects are also subject to a year-end evaluation.

THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 


ENDOWMENT FUND 


2004-2005 
INSPIRING CAMPAIGN RESULTS! 


Since the new campaign was launched for the Endowment Fund on June 8, 2004, twenty-five new members have 
joined the Heritage Club. They have contributed $550,000 in donations, pledges, bequests and in memoriam 
donations. 


Heritage Club members are individuals and families who have demonstrated their attachment to and trust in the 
YMCA by making current or future gifts to the Endowment Fund, namely through their wills or life insurance, or 
by establishing a personalized tribute fund in memory or in honour of a loved one. Their generosity ensures that 
the YMCA will continue to serve Montrealers for many more decades. 


The management of the Endowment Fund has been entrusted to the Foundation of Greater Montreal and is over- 
seen by the Board of Directors of the YMCA of Greater Montreal Foundation. Gifts to the Fund are endowed in 
perpetuity and annual revenues are distributed in accordance with policies adopted by the 
Board of Directors. These policies ensure that even during turbulent market conditions, the 
capital of the Fund is protected and continues to provide a steady source of financial sup- 
port for the community programs offered by the nine YMCA centres and its camp, YMCA 
Kanawana. 


As at May 31, 2005, the market value of the fund was $4.3 million, 
representing an increase of more than 16% compared to the previous year. 


PROJECTS SUPPORTED BY THE ENDOWMENT FUND 


The Endowment Fund provides recurring support for a number of community programs. A portion of annual rev- 
enues (i.e., $39,000) is allocated to programs selected by donors, such as international development and Camp 
YMCA Kanawana. The remaining balance of $63,650 was allocated to special projects selected by an Allocations 
Committee composed of volunteer members of the Board of Directors and YMCA staff. This year, ten applications 
for funding were selected. 


Covered Garden Downtown YMCA Residence $10,000 
Welcoming and supporting refugee claimants and their children 


Healthy Eating Guy-Favreau YMCA $3,000 
Teaching healty eating habits to underprivileged children 


Nature Outing Guy-Favreau YMCA $4,400 
Educational outing for underprivileged children to discover nature 


Circus Arts for Children Pointe-St-Charles YMCA $8,500 
Training to build self-esteem and confidence 


YMCA Youth Festival! Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA $5,000 
Celebrating young talent and initiative 


Co-op Support Loan Program Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA $8,000 
Encouraging self-reliance through financial skills and education 


Teen Fitness Du Pare YMCA $7,500 
Helping youth develop a lifelong exercise habit 


Café 3D Du Parc YMCA $10,000 
A place of development, discovery and downtime for youth 


Sports-Study Girls’ Basketball Du Pare YMCA $3,000 
Helping young girls develop self-esteem through sports and study 


YMCA Conference on International Solidarity $4,250 
International Programs, Association 
Building awareness of global issues

ANNUAL GOLF TOURNAMENT 


The 20th annual golf tournament, which drew 160 people to the Pinegrove 
Golf Club in Saint-Luc on Monday, May 30, 2005 helped raise $87,120. The 
funds were used to finance YMCA Centres’ Youth Programs 
and also the Association-Wide Youth Leadership Program.
